new_statements.rule_in_words: Yongkuk (Tikhakic) is a four-tone language: on the major syllable tone 1 is low falling with creak, tone 2 falling modal, tone 3 high level, tone 4 short and checked. Words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic; the minor syllable (presyllable, e.g. tə- in tə0hɤi1 'blood', ə- in ə0nɐk4 'black') is toneless and unstressed, so prominence sits on the tone-bearing final major syllable (iambic pattern, as in the other Tangsa varieties). No independent word-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. The only competing stress statement for a Tikhakic variety is Chutia 2017 (Longchang, lung1248) ch. III p. 97: compounds 'are subject to a specific compound-stress rule, according to which, stress falls on the third syllable form the end of the formation' — stated for disyllabic tree-name compounds (puzak, pupʰͻk), so internally inconsistent; the thesis has no phonology chapter and the sentence reads as boilerplate. Flagged, not adopted.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms and short phrases elicited from four Yongkuk speakers (Nong Yongkuk, Nong Che, Tulong Yongkuk, Kamtong Kamba), with pitch traces; the 'toneless and unstressed presyllable' sentence is a generalisation over Tangsa-Nocte, applied to Yongkuk in §8.4. Tikhak proper is covered only in comparative tone tables (Table 5.4 p. 104).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.3 tikh1243 'Tikhakic' groups Tikhak (tikh1244), Yongkuk (yong1272), Longchang (lung1248), Kato Naga (kato1246, reported extinct), Nokja (nokj1234) and Kengjung (keng1241). The quoted statement is van Dam's Yongkuk chapter (yong1272) plus his Tangsa-Nocte-general presyllable sentence; Morey 2015 p. 25 says Tikhak and Yongkuk are the most similar members of a mutually intelligible Tikhak group. Tikhak proper (tikh1244) has no published phonology; it appears only in van Dam's comparative tone tables and Morey 2015's tone-marked wordlists. Chutia 2017 describes Longchang (lung1248). Das Gupta 1980 (not opened) also describes Longchang per van Dam p. 177. Khan Lann 2018's 'Yungkuk-Tikhak' grouping also lists Muklum/Havi, which Glottolog keeps separate as Muklomic (mukl1234).

sources.note: §5.1.3 p. 94 (PDF p. 112), for Tangsa-Nocte generally: 'Tangsa-Nocte varieties typically have lexical tone.. The presyllable is toneless and unstressed'. §8.4 Yongkuk pp. 220-225 (PDF pp. 238-243): four tonemes (1 low falling creaky, 2 falling modal, 3 high level, 4 checked); p. 222 'The first syllable is a sesquisyllabic prefix which is atonal.' No word-stress rule is given for Yongkuk or Tikhak; Tikhak proper appears only in comparative tone tables (Table 5.4 p. 104) and in the geography/classification discussion (p. 177: Das Gupta 1980 described Longchang).
